description: The trunk of the tree: the deep branches every other file hangs from.

nodes.name: LUCA
nodes.summary: The Last Universal Common Ancestor: a single-celled population living around 4.2 billion years ago from which every living thing — bacteria, mushrooms, oak trees and you — descends.
facts: LUCA probably lived near hot hydrothermal vents on the sea floor.
It already had DNA, ribosomes and a genetic code that every organism still shares today.
LUCA was not the first life — just the last ancestor all survivors have in common.

nodes.name: Bacteria
nodes.summary: Tiny cells with no nucleus. Bacteria are everywhere — in soil, oceans, clouds and your gut — and outnumber the stars in the observable universe.
facts: Your body holds roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells.
Some bacteria survive boiling, freezing and even the vacuum of space.

nodes.name: Cyanobacteria
nodes.summary: The first organisms to split water using sunlight and release oxygen. They changed the atmosphere forever and later became the chloroplasts inside every plant.
facts: Every breath you take is thanks to oxygen first made by cyanobacteria.
They built stromatolites — rocky microbial reefs that still grow in Shark Bay, Australia.

nodes.name: Alphaproteobacteria
nodes.summary: A class of bacteria that includes the ancestor of mitochondria — the power stations inside your cells.
facts: Mitochondria still carry their own small circle of bacterial DNA.

nodes.name: Archaea
nodes.summary: Microbes that look like bacteria but run on very different chemistry. Many thrive in boiling springs, salt lakes and the guts of cows.
facts: Archaea were only recognised as a separate domain of life in 1977.
Methane-making archaea in cow stomachs are a significant source of greenhouse gas.

nodes.name: Asgard archaea
nodes.summary: Deep-sea archaea named after the home of the Norse gods. They carry genes once thought unique to complex cells, and are our closest microbial relatives.
facts: The first Asgard archaea were found in mud near a hydrothermal vent called Loki's Castle.
Their discovery suggests complex cells grew out of an archaeon that swallowed a bacterium.

nodes.name: Complex cells
nodes.summary: Cells with a nucleus and mitochondria. They formed when an Asgard archaeon teamed up with a bacterium that became the mitochondrion — the most important merger in history.
facts: All animals, plants and fungi are eukaryotes.
This partnership, called endosymbiosis, gave cells enough energy to become large and complex.

nodes.name: Amorphea
nodes.summary: A huge supergroup uniting amoebas, fungi and animals — the side of the eukaryote family tree that we belong to.

nodes.name: Opisthokonts
nodes.summary: Fungi, animals and their single-celled relatives. Their swimming cells push themselves with a single tail at the back — just like sperm.
facts: This is why a mushroom is more closely related to you than to a tree.

nodes.name: Fungi
nodes.summary: Mushrooms, moulds and yeasts. Fungi digest food outside their bodies and weave vast underground networks that feed forests.
facts: One honey fungus in Oregon covers nearly 10 square kilometres — possibly the largest organism on Earth.
Fungal cell walls are made of chitin, the same material as insect shells.

nodes.name: Animals
nodes.summary: Multicellular organisms that eat other living things and, mostly, move. Animals likely began as simple filter-feeding blobs in ancient seas.
facts: Molecular clocks suggest animals arose long before they left clear fossils.
There may be around 7 million animal species, most of them insects.

nodes.name: Diaphoretickes
nodes.summary: The other great half of complex life: plants, algae and a dazzling variety of single-celled protists.

nodes.name: SAR supergroup
nodes.summary: An enormous group of protists including giant kelp, glassy diatoms, the malaria parasite and shell-building foraminifera.

nodes.name: Archaeplastida
nodes.summary: Red algae, green algae and land plants. Their ancestor swallowed a cyanobacterium and, instead of digesting it, kept it as a solar panel: the chloroplast.
facts: Every leaf's green colour comes from those captured bacteria.

nodes.name: Green plants
nodes.summary: Green algae and all land plants. They feed nearly every food chain on land.

nodes.name: Bilaterians
nodes.summary: Animals with a left and right side, a head end and a tail end — and a gut running through. From worms to whales.

nodes.name: Protostomes
nodes.summary: Insects, spiders, snails, octopuses and worms. In their embryos the first opening becomes the mouth.

nodes.name: Deuterostomes
nodes.summary: Starfish, sea urchins and all vertebrates. In their embryos the first opening becomes the bottom — the mouth forms second.
facts: Yes: you are more closely related to a starfish than to an octopus.

nodes.name: Chordates
nodes.summary: Animals with a stiff rod (notochord) along the back, a nerve cord above it and gill slits — at least as embryos.

nodes.name: Vertebrates
nodes.summary: Animals with a backbone and a skull. The first were small, jawless, fish-like swimmers in Cambrian seas.

nodes.name: Jawed vertebrates
nodes.summary: Jaws evolved from gill arches and transformed vertebrates into powerful predators.
facts: The tiny bones in your middle ear evolved from ancient jaw bones.

nodes.name: Bony fish
nodes.summary: Fish with bony skeletons. They split into ray-finned fish — most fish today — and lobe-finned fish, our ancestors.

nodes.name: Lobe-finned fish
nodes.summary: Fish with fleshy, bony fins — the bones that would become our arms and legs.

nodes.name: Tetrapodomorphs
nodes.summary: Lobe-finned fish on the road to land: their fins grew wrists, their necks grew flexible and their lungs grew stronger.

nodes.name: Tetrapods
nodes.summary: Four-limbed vertebrates. Amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals all descend from fish that crawled out of Devonian swamps.

nodes.name: Amniotes
nodes.summary: Animals whose eggs carry their own private pond — the amnion — so they could finally breed far from water.

nodes.name: Sauropsids
nodes.summary: The reptile line: lizards, snakes, turtles, crocodiles, dinosaurs and birds.

nodes.name: Synapsids
nodes.summary: The mammal line, recognised by a single opening behind the eye socket. Early synapsids like Dimetrodon were not dinosaurs — they were our ancestors' cousins.
